1394.title: Mahabali, the asura devotee

1394.howItsDone: At Onam, families in Kerala remember Mahabali's reign with songs, flower designs at the door and a shared feast, and the Bhagavata Purana's account of Bali and Vamana is retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herath: Shiva's night ends in shared prasad, the soaked walnuts carried door to door. Today, the far southwest.

When Maveli ruled the land, everyone was alike. That's the opening, in paraphrase, of a folk song sung in Kerala at Onam. It goes on: there was no theft and no cheating, not even a small lie. Nobody was in trouble, and nobody was afraid. It sounds like a children's daydream. But the king in the song isn't a god. He's an asura, from the side of the stories usually cast as the gods' rivals. And he was so good at being king that heaven itself got nervous.
screen: `A SONG ABOUT A GOOD KING` → `NO THEFT, NO LIES` → `A KING FROM THE OTHER SIDE`

segments.voice: Year one gave you Onam: a king's yearly homecoming. Here is the king. His name is Bali, and Kerala calls him Mahabali, great Bali, or Maveli for short. His story is told in the Bhagavata Purana. He's the grandson of Prahlada, the boy devotee who held to Vishnu through every danger. Bali is generous, devout and strong, and with the help of his teacher Shukra, he wins the three worlds, heaven included. The gods are pushed out. Their mother, Aditi, grieves for them and prays. And notice what the text does not say. It never calls Bali cruel. His problem isn't wickedness. A good man is sitting on a throne that isn't his. Vishnu answers Aditi's prayer by being born as her son, Vamana, a small brahmin boy. He walks to Bali's great sacrifice, where the king is giving gifts to anyone who asks. Bali welcomes him warmly: ask for anything. And the boy asks only for as much ground as he can cover in three of his own steps. Bali calls it a child's request. Now the teaching under the story. Hindu stories don't split the world into a good team and a bad team. Asuras are usually the gods' rivals, yet the Bhagavata names Bali, and his grandfather Prahlada, among its twelve mahajanas, the great ones who truly know the path of devotion. What makes someone great is devotion and dharma, not the side they were born on. That's why a whole festival in Kerala can long for an asura king.
screen: `MAHABALI, GRANDSON OF PRAHLADA` · `A GOOD KING ON A THRONE NOT HIS` · `VAMANA ASKS FOR THREE STEPS` · then, large: `DEVOTION, NOT SIDES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'd usually put on the other side: another school, another team, another way of seeing the world. Hold them for a minute the way the Bhagavata holds Bali, as someone whose goodness might be real. Rest with the breath. If you pray, you can say Om Namo Narayanaya softly, a prayer to Vishnu many Hindus say, the god both Prahlada and Bali loved.

1395.title: Bali keeps his word
1395.hook: a teacher warns the king that the small boy is Vishnu, and the king keeps his promise anyway
1395.carry: truth kept, and the self offered to God
1395.tomorrow: where does a god send the king who gave him everything?
1395.howItsDone: At Onam, Keralites retell how Mahabali kept his word to Vamana and offered his head for the third step, and the Bhagavata Purana's account of it is read and recited in the season.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: devotion counts, not the side you're born on. Bali, the asura devotee, smiled at a small boy who asked for three steps of ground.

The water pot is already tilted. In the old way of giving a gift, the giver pours water to seal the promise, and Bali is about to pour. Then his teacher, Shukra, pulls him aside. Shukra sees what the king doesn't: that small boy is Vishnu. Give him three steps and he will take everything you have. Take your word back, he says. Here, even a teacher thinks a lie would be wiser. Today, what a good king does with a promise that's about to cost him the world.
screen: `THE WATER POT TILTED` → `SHUKRA'S WARNING` → `A PROMISE THAT WILL COST`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana gives Shukra a strong case. He tells Bali that this boy is Vishnu in disguise, and that the gift will strip him of everything. He even argues that in some moments, an untrue word is allowed. Bali hears him out, and refuses. In paraphrase: I am Prahlada's grandson. I have said I will give. I will not take it back. And the text puts a striking line in his mouth: the earth can carry any weight except the weight of a liar. So Bali pours the water. Shukra, angry, curses him to lose his fortune. Then the small boy begins to grow, past the trees, past the sky, until he holds the worlds inside his body. With one step he covers the earth. With the second, the heavens. There's nowhere left for the third. Bali's soldiers rush at the giant, and Bali stops them. He is bound with ropes. And Vamana asks: where does my third step go? Bali answers: put it on my head. Hindu teachers hear two teachings here. The first is satya, truth, one of the oldest pillars of dharma: for Bali, a broken word weighs more than three lost worlds. The second is bhakti at its deepest. In the Bhagavata, Prahlada lists nine ways of loving God, from hearing God's name to offering your whole self. Many Vaishnava teachers name Bali as the great example of that last one, atma-nivedana, the self offered. He bowed his head, and let God's foot rest on it.

segments.voice: Hold one promise you've made that's still open, to a friend, a parent, God, yourself, the way Bali held the water pot. Ask quietly what keeping it would cost, and what breaking it would cost. Then breathe out and let your head bow a little, the way Bali bowed his. If you pray, offer the day with that bow.

1396.title: Vishnu at Bali's door
1396.hook: a king who lost everything gets a guard at his door, and a visit home that Kerala gets ready for
1396.carry: grace took the throne, then guarded the door
1396.tomorrow: a baby cries by a river, a bell at his neck. whose son is he?
1396.howItsDone: At Onam, families in Kerala lay a pookalam of flower petals at the door, wear new clothes and share the sadya, a feast served on a banana leaf, to welcome Mahabali on his visit to his people.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: truth kept, and the self offered to God. Warned by his teacher, Bali kept his word and bowed his head for the third step.

Where do you send a king who has just lost the three worlds? Bali was left bound, his head under the foot of the giant Vamana. A story could end there, with the proud one humbled. The Bhagavata Purana doesn't. And Kerala doesn't either. On an Onam morning in Kerala, someone is on their knees at the front door, laying flower petals into a circle, ring by ring. In the way Kerala tells it, they're getting ready for a guest.
screen: `BALI BOUND` → `FLOWERS BEFORE DAWN` → `READY FOR A GUEST`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata, Bali's grandfather Prahlada arrives, and Bali's wife pleads for him. And Vishnu explains himself. When I favor someone, he says, I take away their wealth, because pride in wealth makes a person stiff, deaf to the world and to me. Hindus call God's favor anugraha, grace, and here it looks exactly like loss. Then Vishnu gives Bali a new home, a realm under the earth called Sutala, a place of comfort and peace. And he makes a startling promise: he will stand at Bali's door himself, mace in hand, guarding him. The god who took the worlds becomes the doorkeeper of the king who gave them. Teachers love this picture: God, who needs nothing, bound by love to a devotee. Here Kerala adds what the Bhagavata doesn't say. Tradition in Kerala says Bali asked for one more thing: to come back and see his people once a year. Onam is that visit. So people get ready the way you'd get ready for someone you love, and the way the Upanishads say to treat any guest: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. The flower carpet at the door is the pookalam. The great meal, the sadya, is served on a banana leaf, dish after dish in its place, and families sit down together to eat it. New clothes, games, boat races, songs. Losing the throne wasn't the end of Bali. In this telling, it was grace.
screen: `I TAKE THE WEALTH OF THOSE I FAVOR` · `SUTALA: A NEW HOME` · `VISHNU GUARDS BALI'S DOOR` · `THE GUEST IS GOD` · then, large: `ANUGRAHA: GRACE.`

segments.voice: With each slow breath, lay down one ring of petals, the way a pookalam is built from the center out: one ring for the people in your home, one for your street, one for someone you haven't seen in a long time. Keep going until the circle feels wide enough, then rest in the middle of it. If you pray, offer the circle to Vishnu, who keeps Bali's door.
Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, Bali's reward: Vishnu guards his door, and Kerala welcomes him home each Onam with flowers and a feast. Today's word.
Your line: grace took the throne, then guarded the door. The god who took the worlds stands guard for the giver. Flowers at the door, and that's today.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: grace took the throne, then guarded the door. That's Onam. Today the week turns from Onam to Ayyappa, the god of a forest hill.

A crying sound, thin and high, somewhere near the river. The king of Pandalam is out hunting in the forest, and he stops his horse to listen. It isn't a bird. He follows the sound down to the bank of the Pampa, and there, alone on the ground, is a baby boy, bright as a lamp, with a small bell tied around his neck. No mother. No hut. No one. And the king has no children of his own.
screen: `A CRY BY THE RIVER` → `A BABY WITH A BELL` → `A KING WITH NO CHILDREN`

segments.voice: In the story as it's told in Kerala, a demoness named Mahishi has won a boon that makes her almost impossible to defeat. Only a son born of Shiva and Vishnu together could overcome her, which sounds like a riddle with no answer. Here's the answer. Vishnu once took the form of Mohini, an enchanting woman, and from Shiva and Mohini a child is born. So Ayyappa is called Hariharaputra, the son of Hari and Hara: Hari is a name of Vishnu, Hara a name of Shiva. That matters. Hindus have long had Shaivas, devoted above all to Shiva, and Vaishnavas, devoted above all to Vishnu, and at times the two argued hard. The tradition keeps answering back. Old temples carve Harihara, one figure, half Shiva and half Vishnu, as in the caves at Badami, and many teachers say Hari and Hara are one. Ayyappa makes it a family: one child with both of them as parents. The baby is left by the river Pampa with a bell at his neck. The childless king of Pandalam finds him and longs to keep him. In the telling, a holy man tells the king: raise him as your son, and the truth will come out in time. So they call him Manikandan, which the story explains as the one with the bell at his throat. The son of two gods grows up as an adopted prince, loved by a father who doesn't yet know who he is.

segments.voice: Let the breath settle. If you don't pray, let the in-breath and the out-breath be two halves of one circle, and rest where they join.

The prescription is impossible on purpose. The queen of Pandalam lies in a darkened room, clutching her head. The palace physician bows and gives his verdict: only one cure will work, the milk of a tigress. The room goes silent. Nobody walks into the forest and milks a tiger, and the physician knows it. Because the illness, in the story, isn't real. It's a plan to send someone into the forest who isn't supposed to come back. Today, the boy who went anyway.

segments.voice: In the telling, after the king adopts Manikandan, the queen has a son of her own. A scheming minister whispers to her that the adopted boy will take the throne from her child. Afraid, she agrees to pretend to be ill, and the physician is in on it. Manikandan is still young. He hears what the cure is, and he offers to go. The king begs him not to. The boy goes anyway, alone, into the forest, with a bundle of food for the road. He simply goes to fetch what his mother says she needs. In the forest, tradition says, he meets the demoness Mahishi and overcomes her, which was why he was born. Then he comes home, not with a pot of milk, but riding on a tigress, with tigers walking behind him. The queen and the minister, seeing him, understand what they've done, and fall at his feet. And here the story puts its weight. Not on punishment, but on forgiveness. Manikandan forgives them, and tells the king who he is and why he came. Hindu teachers rank forgiveness high: in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna lists kshama, forgiveness, among the divine qualities, the marks of a person turned toward God. The god of the forest hill answers a trap with care, and the people who set it with pardon. Notice who he forgives: not a stranger, but family, the one who should have kept him safe. That's the hardest kind, and the story says that's where the divine shows most.
screen: `A PLAN BORN OF FEAR` · `THE BOY GOES ANYWAY` · `HOME ON A TIGRESS` · `HE FORGIVES THEM` · then, large: `KSHAMA: A DIVINE QUALITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who once set you up, or wished you less than well. Don't force forgiveness, and forgiving never means staying where you're still being hurt. Just hold their face a breath longer than you want to, the way Manikandan stood before the queen, breathing in steadiness and breathing out the grudge. If you pray, say Ayyappa's pilgrims' chant softly with each breath: Swamiye saranam Ayyappa.
Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, the tiger's milk: a cure meant as a trap, a boy who went anyway, his return on a tigress, and his pardon. Today's word.

Swami. A man in a black dhoti says it to the tea seller at the bottom of the hill. The tea seller says it back. A pilgrim with gray hair says it to a teenager who's stopped to catch his breath, and the teenager says it to him. On the forest path up to Sabarimala, it's how people greet each other, thank each other, ask each other to move aside. Swami: the word for a master, a holy one, the Lord, used for everyone. Today, the pilgrimage up Ayyappa's hill.
screen: `SWAMI, SAID TO EVERYONE` → `A FOREST PATH UP A HILL` → `THE NAME EVERY PILGRIM SHARES`

segments.voice: Tradition says that when Manikandan's work on earth was done, he shot an arrow and asked that his temple be built where it fell. It fell on a hill in the forest: Sabarimala, where Ayyappa is worshiped seated in meditation. Pilgrims don't just set out. For a season before the climb they keep a vow. They wear a bead necklace, dress in black or dark blue, eat simple food, give up alcohol, keep celibacy, and often walk barefoot. From the day the necklace goes on, the pilgrim is called swami, and even Ayyappa, by name. Each pilgrim climbs with the irumudi on the head, a cloth bundle tied in two parts: one carries offerings, including a coconut filled with ghee for the god; the other, food for the road. The forest echoes with a chant: Swamiye saranam Ayyappa, Lord, you are my refuge, Ayyappa. On the way, pilgrims stop at Erumeli, where Ayyappa's companion in the stories, a Muslim named Vavar, is honored too. Rich and poor wear the same dark cloth and answer to the same name. Tradition says that above the shrine are the words tat tvam asi, that thou art, from the Upanishads. Here's the teaching. In the Upanishads, it means the self in you, the atman, is one with Brahman, the divine in everything. The pilgrimage acts it out. If the god lives in every pilgrim, the right word for the stranger beside you is swami.
screen: `WHERE THE ARROW FELL` · `A SEASON OF VOWS` · `THE IRUMUDI ON THE HEAD` · `THAT THOU ART` · then, large: `ATMAN IS BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Breathe in slowly, and on each out-breath take one step up a forest hill in your mind. Each time a face comes to mind, someone easy or someone hard, greet them inwardly the pilgrim's way: swami. If you pray, you can say the pilgrims' chant, Swamiye saranam Ayyappa, softly, in time with the steps.

Bare feet on a mountain path, high in the Himalayas. A boy, thin from fasting, wearing only a loincloth, carrying a staff, a string of beads and a small bundle. No family with him. In the stories his followers tell, he left home young, and he's been walking ever since, from one holy place to the next, looking for something. People along the road call him Nilkanth. Today, a new region, Gujarat, and the walk that brought this boy there.
screen: `BARE FEET IN THE HIMALAYAS` → `A BOY WITH A STAFF` → `NILKANTH, WALKING`

segments.voice: Tradition says he was born Ghanshyam, in a village called Chhapaiya, not far from Ayodhya in the north. After his parents died, he left home as a young renunciant, a brahmachari, and took the name Nilkanth, blue-throat, one of the names of Shiva. His followers tell of a long journey on foot across India: the Himalayas, the holy sites of the east, the temples of the south, hard austerities, yogi after yogi, and moving on from each. He wasn't wandering for its own sake. He was asking questions and not settling for half answers. At last he comes west, into Gujarat, to a small ashram at a village called Loj. It belongs to a teacher named Ramanand Swami, and his disciple Muktanand receives the young stranger. Nilkanth asks his questions: about the soul, about God, about the world and what binds us to it. Followers tell that the answers satisfied him, and this time he stays. Here's the teaching under the walk. In Hinduism the deepest knowledge is received from a guru. The Mundaka Upanishad tells the seeker to go, fuel for the fire in hand, to a teacher who knows the scriptures and stands firm in Brahman. That's the seed of the Swaminarayan tradition, a living Hindu community with deep roots in Gujarat. And it's why so many Hindu families still say: for the questions that matter most, don't stop at the first answer you find. Find someone who has walked the road, and learn at their feet.
screen: `GHANSHYAM BECOMES NILKANTH` · `A WALK ACROSS INDIA` · `ARRIVING AT LOJ IN GUJARAT` · then, large: `GO TO A GURU.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, as if you had a staff in your hand, and let a real question come up, one you haven't finished with, about God, about yourself, about what matters. Don't answer it; let it walk with you, breath after breath, the way Nilkanth carried his questions from place to place. If you pray, hold the question as a prayer, and ask to be led to the right teacher.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, Nilkanth: the boy born Ghanshyam, who walked across India with his questions until he reached Ramanand Swami's ashram at Loj. Today's word.
